title: What you suggest from moving from Codex to Claude?
author: kuroshikigami_
selftext:
I am currently building several projects in codex and after seeing significant improvements in Claude Opus, I have decided to move my projects from one AI to another. How would you go about this as I have coding already in place? 

I do most designs by myself but the programming aspect is not in my wheelhouse. So I'm currently stuck in that aspect... 

The reason I ask is that the base of my primary project is already significantly developed but still needs 3d assets, player interactions, game AI and online features... What would you suggest?

comments.author: Monecreiff
comments.body: I asked claude and she said not too

comments.author: Sleepnotdeading
comments.body:
Before making any changes, I'd show the codebase to Claude Code, and have it map the project, and the project roadmap for upcoming features.  Then I'd show that map to Codex and have it verify, and/or make any notes or corrections.

I've never migrated a projects between AIs but I don't think there's too much to it beyond a mindful handoff between the two models.

replies.author: ImCallingYouOutOnBS
replies.body:
Yuup, I have a custom game dev framework and engine built on a forked and heavily modified version of Godot, and I have it setup so that every single tool, function, and feature has a dock with explicitly instructions on how to use them, and their limitations. 

This is how I could plug basically any AI into my project, in the case that for example, anthropic decides out of nowhere to double their prices. 

Nothing I built is soley by AI, it's made by a tool that I give the AI plugged in explicit instructions on how to use

replies.author: kuroshikigami_
replies.body: Would it make sense to integrate a "project tracker" that links to the goals.md and agents.md? That way it can liaise? Or?

comments.author: 17BelowGames
comments.body: I’ll be honest, I keep both and have them work out of a GitHub repository in issues they review each others work and suggest edits to each other. I think Claude is more efficient with token usage and codex is more detail oriented when it comes to its code.

replies.author: kuroshikigami_
replies.body: Never considered that being such a major difference between the two. It's more that after seeing so many posts on Claude Opus versus sol 6.1 that it might be more effective at what I want to do and what I have planned.

replies.author: 17BelowGames
replies.body: It does come down to what you need them for my game Claude is better at pixel art using lua scripts and aseprite, codex is better at implementing the code for the mechanics in the game. I noticed Claude would sometimes make static references which codex would catch during reviews. I personally use both and have actually had a better experience in making games now.

comments.author: heavy-minium
comments.body:
There is normally only very little to account for when switching AI agents.

If your main instructions are in a [AGENTS.md](http://AGENTS.md), it gets picked up by both. Skills for Claude Code unfortunately still need to be in a ".claude" folder instead of ".agents". And that's it, really, nothing much changes. Personally I use Codex, Claude Code and GitHub Copilot all at the same time, I just make a symbolic link of ".agents" to ".claude" to keep both in sync, and otherwise share all the same setup.

You don't sound like someone who would have heavily customized their agents with hooks and whatsnot, so that can probably be ignored.

The potential pitfall that may come on top are however if you over-relied on the memory feature of the specific AI agent, instead of having things memorized and tracked within a project. There could be a lot of very important stuff in there. Your past conversations themselves might be a treasure trove of important details that the other agent would not have access to, unless you explicitly tell it to look at those files. Which is why it's recommended to not even let this happen in the first place, don't let agents rely too much on info from past conversations or memory.

replies.author: kuroshikigami_
replies.body:
Okay, that sounds feasible. I was running with one coordinator and 3 subagents basing off what the coordinator was advising. 

I am unsure what you mean by hooks but if you mean limitations, then I have imposed a lot but in my game design bible. 

My main 3 issues are:
- I have designed and developed a number of assets for my game and they have this comely low poly vibe that would be nice in a low poly game but I want them more realistic (so I'm trying different PBX textures) but no matter how I try, the "damage" simulation where they fall apart depending on where and how they sustained damage is... Failing... 
- I made a 2d map to 3d asset procedural generator where I can draw on a real map the assets required and the direction of the assets but it doesn't recognise the markings for roads, buildings etc... so when I procedurally generate the map, it fails... Epically... 
- the lighting system is too bright and I need it to flutter, flicker or turn off occasionally for an eerie vibe at times. 

Would you happen to have any advice? Do you think having Claude look at it from a different perspective would help?

replies.author: heavy-minium
replies.body:
>I have designed and developed a number of assets for my game and they have this comely low poly vibe that would be nice in a low poly game but I want them more realistic (so I'm trying different PBX textures) but no matter how I try, the "damage" simulation where they fall apart depending on where and how they sustained damage is... Failing...

Well, I could certainly help here, but it's wild guesses unless you specify what's failing. The term to look and ask AI for is mesh fracturing. What you generally want to do is to prepare a fractured version of the mesh in advance. The non-fractured version is sleeping and not interacting with physics. Once it starts fracturing, you switch to the fractured version, make it participate in physics. Don't expect too much out of this, it is a difficult discipline to get this more and more realistic and performat enough. Down to mapping PBR textures correctly to the fractured parts, and having multiple levels of fracturation, as well as using a convicing way of splitting up meshes that may have non-trivial configuration (convex/concave), with performant collision shapes that don't feel weird, this is absolutely not an easy thing to do, and very hard if you don't know what to ask the AI for. Destructions are one of the most "faked" aspects of videogame development - often development give up on simulating it in the engine and will instead use software like Houdini to perform the simulation offline, and then only export an asset that is one fixed variation of one of multiple possible, but limited number, of "destructed" configurations.

>I made a 2d map to 3d asset procedural generator where I can draw on a real map the assets required and the direction of the assets but it doesn't recognise the markings for roads, buildings etc... so when I procedurally generate the map, it fails... Epically...

You'd have to share more details here, there are widly different guesses to make about what this could mean. One general thing to not is that you can probably forget about the direction of an assets being reliably deduce from a 2D map. You're better of combining 2D map for terrain with 3D placement of assets in an in-game editor, for example.

>the lighting system is too bright and I need it to flutter, flicker or turn off occasionally for an eerie vibe at times.

>Ask AI to expose the parameters in a UI. Play around with those settings, tell AI which settings you want for a specific situation/area of the map.

>

Would you happen to have any advice? Do you think having Claude look at it from a different perspective would help?

No, actually the AI agent ain't gonna make much difference for the cases you mentioned, it's more about knowledge and how you describe what you want the AI to do - and also knowing when a specific approach is going nowhere and unfixable. One thing you should pay attention to is when pointing out visible issues, is to take a screenshot of that specific area and to frame the area of interest. Like "I encircled the problematic area in red in the screenshot". Make sure to use a model like Sol, Opus, Astra at least at the default effort level when giving it screenshots, because the accuracy of their vision capabilities scale with model and effort. Try to avoid a bigger screenshot than necessary, so that it's really well "zoomed" in, but with enough around the area of issue for the AI to understand the context of what it is looking at.
